- When sentiment is consistently positive (≥0.67) over recent days, model tends to overestimate and should reduce forecast slope or add downward bias.
- When sentiment is consistently negative (≤0.33) or neutral (0.00), model often underestimates and should adjust upward, especially if recent price is falling.
- After sharp price spikes (e.g., >10% from prior day), model frequently overshoots and should apply a “cool-down” correction — reduce forecast by 1–2% per day for 3–5 days.
- If model forecast is flat or rising slowly but true outcome shows strong mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 consecutive days of decline), reduce forecast slope and add downward drift.
- For 30-day horizon, if true outcome deviates >5% from model’s initial forecast, adjust for sentiment-driven volatility — e.g., if sentiment is volatile (alternating 0.33/1.00), add ±1–2% buffer to forecast.
- If sentiment history shows “reversal” (e.g., 0.33 → 1.00 → 0.33), model often fails to anticipate reversal — reduce forecast slope after sentiment shift to 0.33 or below.
- When true outcome is significantly lower than model (e.g., >10% drop), check if sentiment was negative — if so, model may be “overconfident” and should be scaled down by 1–3% per day for 3–5 days.
- If model forecast is rising steadily but true outcome shows early sharp drop (e.g., first 3–5 days), apply “early correction” — reduce forecast by 1–2% per day for first 3 days.
